title: Cache Performance Analysis: AMAT and the Memory Hierarchy

sections.heading: Three numbers and one equation
sections.body:
Cache performance is governed by three quantities. **Miss rate** $m$ is the fraction of memory references that miss — misses divided by accesses, equivalently $1$ minus the hit rate. CENG331 quotes typical figures of 3–10% for an L1 cache and, depending on size, well under 1% for an L2. **Hit time** $T_h$ is the time to deliver a line that *is* present, including set selection, tag comparison and word selection — not merely the data transfer; the slides give 1–2 cycles for a generic L1 and 5–20 cycles for a generic L2. **Miss penalty** $T_p$ is the *additional* time a miss costs on top of $T_h$ — 50 to 200 cycles to main memory on the systems the course models, with the trend increasing because DRAM latency has not kept pace with clock speed.

The average memory access time combines them:

$$\text{AMAT} = T_h + m \cdot T_p .$$

The asymmetry is the entire content of the formula: $T_h$ is paid on *every* reference — a miss is only detected once the lookup has already failed — while $T_p$ is paid on the fraction $m$ of references that miss. This is also why the course insists on quoting miss rate rather than hit rate. With $T_h = 1$ cycle and $T_p = 100$ cycles, a 97%-hit cache gives $\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.03 \times 100 = 4$ cycles, while a 99%-hit cache gives $1 + 0.01 \times 100 = 2$ cycles: two points of hit rate halve the access time, because $\partial\,\text{AMAT}/\partial m = T_p$ is large. Hit rate compresses exactly the region where the interesting variation lives.

sections.heading: Multi-level caches: the AMAT recursion
sections.body:
With several cache levels, the miss penalty of level $k$ is not a fixed constant — it is the average access time of level $k+1$:

$$\text{AMAT}_k = T_{h,k} + m_k \cdot \text{AMAT}_{k+1},$$

bottoming out at $\text{AMAT}_{\text{last}+1} = T_{\text{DRAM}}$. Here $m_k$ is the **local** miss rate: misses at level $k$ divided by the references that actually reached level $k$ (i.e., that already missed at every level above). Expanding the recursion gives an equivalent flat sum in terms of the **global** miss rate $g_k = m_1 m_2 \cdots m_k$, the fraction of *all* CPU references that miss all the way down through level $k$:

$$\text{AMAT} = T_{h,1} + \sum_{k \ge 1} g_k\,T_{h,k+1}.$$

Conflating local and global rates is the most common error on this material. A local L2 miss rate of 25–40% sounds alarming, but it is normal: L1 has already filtered out every easy hit, so what reaches L2 is the hard residue. Only the corresponding global rate says anything about the program as a whole, and it is a fraction of a percent. CENG334's treatment of AMAT for the virtual-memory case makes the same point with different labels, $\text{AMAT} = P_{\text{hit}}\,T_M + P_{\text{miss}}\,T_D$ for memory versus disk: the structure is identical, a weighted average of a cheap path and an expensive one, just applied one level lower in the hierarchy where $T_D$ is measured in milliseconds instead of cycles.

sections.heading: What block size and associativity trade away
sections.body:
Every cache parameter buys something by spending something else. A **larger block** exploits spatial locality and drives the compulsory miss rate down — for a stride-1 scan it is exactly $\text{sizeof(elem)}/B$ — but for a fixed cache size it leaves fewer lines, which hurts programs with more temporal than spatial locality, and it lengthens the transfer, which raises the miss penalty rather than the miss rate. Modern designs, including the Core i7, settle on 64-byte blocks as the compromise.

**Higher associativity** reduces the cache's vulnerability to thrashing from conflict misses — with blocks restricted to a single set, a reference stream like $0, 8, 0, 8, \ldots$ striking one set can miss on every access even though the cache is nearly empty. But associativity is expensive: more tag bits and replacement-state bits per line, and more parallel comparators, which can raise both the hit time (more logic on the critical path) and the miss penalty (choosing a victim among more lines takes longer). The resulting trade-off is between hit time and miss penalty, and it explains why real hierarchies are shaped the way they are: low associativity near the top, where the miss penalty is only a few cycles and hit time dominates, and higher associativity further down, where a miss is already expensive and a few extra cycles of lookup barely register. The Core i7 follows this pattern exactly — 8-way at L1 and L2, 16-way at L3.

sections.heading: The Intel Core i7 cache hierarchy
sections.body:
CENG331 works with the Core i7 as its concrete example of the whole picture. Each of the four cores has a private 32 KB, 8-way L1 instruction cache and a private 32 KB, 8-way L1 data cache, each at 4 cycles' access time; a private 256 KB, 8-way unified L2 at 11 cycles; and all cores share an 8 MB, 16-way unified L3 at 30–40 cycles. Every level uses 64-byte blocks, and the entire hierarchy is on the CPU package, backed by main memory.

From $C = S \times E \times B$, the number of sets follows directly: the L1 has $S = 32768/(8 \times 64) = 64$ sets, so 6 index bits and 6 block-offset bits address every byte inside it. The L2 has $S = 262144/(8 \times 64) = 512$ sets (9 index bits), and the L3 has $S = 8388608/(16 \times 64) = 8192$ sets (13 index bits) — an order of magnitude more sets at each level down, which is how capacity grows without a proportional growth in comparators per set. On the i7 the 12 low bits of an address (6 index + 6 offset for L1) coincide with the page offset, which virtual and physical addresses share, so the L1 lookup can start from the virtual address while the TLB is still translating the rest.

sections.heading: From the model to loop order
sections.body: The model becomes actionable the moment it predicts a miss rate from a loop nest. C stores arrays in row-major order, so `a[i][j]` sits at $\text{base} + (i \cdot N + j)\cdot\text{sizeof(elem)}$. Walking the inner index `j` is a stride-1 scan: once every $B/\text{sizeof(elem)}$ elements a new block is touched, giving compulsory miss rate $\text{sizeof(elem)}/B$. Walking `i` instead strides by $N \cdot \text{sizeof(elem)}$ bytes; once that exceeds the block size, every access lands in a fresh block and the miss rate is 1 — no spatial locality survives at all. The course's matrix-multiply example fixes $B = 32$ bytes (four 64-bit words), assumes $N$ large enough that $1/N \approx 0$, and assumes the cache too small to hold multiple rows, so only same-block reuse within one row or column can ever hit; reading the access pattern of each loop order's inner loop then gives its miss rate directly — 0.25 for a stride-1 reference, 1.0 for a stride-$N$ one, a fourfold difference in memory traffic for identical arithmetic. Interchanging loops only fixes spatial locality; reusing a whole working set (as in blocking, where matrices are processed in tiles small enough to stay resident across an inner loop) is what exploits temporal locality on top of it.

complexity.notes: 6 index + 6 offset bits overlap the page offset
Local L2 miss rates of 25–40% are ordinary
Dominant AMAT term once the global miss rate $g_3$ is non-negligible

code.caption: Verifies the compulsory-miss-rate prediction from the matrix-multiply slides: stride-1 traversal should miss at sizeof(elem)/B, stride-N traversal at 1.0.

worked_example.problem:
Using the Core i7 parameters from the CENG331 slides — L1 d-cache 32 KB/8-way, L2 256 KB/8-way, L3 8 MB/16-way, all with 64-byte blocks, and a 52-bit physical address (40-bit PPN + 12-bit PPO, from the address-translation slides):

1. Derive the tag / set-index / block-offset bit widths for the L1 and L2 caches.
2. Take hit times $T_{h,1}=4$, $T_{h,2}=11$, $T_{h,3}=35$ cycles (the midpoint of the slides' 30–40 range) and a main-memory access of $T_{\text{DRAM}}=200$ cycles. With local miss rates $m_1=5\%$, $m_2=30\%$, $m_3=45\%$, compute AMAT by the recursion, then verify it against the flat global-miss-rate form.
worked_example.solution:
**1. Address breakdown.** From $C = S \times E \times B$:

$$S_{L1} = \frac{32768}{8 \times 64} = 64 = 2^6 \ \Rightarrow\ s=6 \text{ index bits}, \quad b = \log_2 64 = 6 \text{ offset bits}.$$

With a 52-bit physical address, the tag is $t = 52 - 6 - 6 = 40$ bits — exactly the 40-bit cache tag (CT) the address-translation slides show for the L1 d-cache, alongside a 6-bit cache index (CI) and 6-bit offset. For the L2:

$$S_{L2} = \frac{262144}{8 \times 64} = 512 = 2^9 \ \Rightarrow\ s=9, \quad b=6, \quad t = 52 - 9 - 6 = 37 \text{ bits}.$$

**2. AMAT.** Unwind the recursion from the bottom:

$$\text{AMAT}_3 = 35 + 0.45 \times 200 = 125 \text{ cycles}$$

$$\text{AMAT}_2 = 11 + 0.30 \times 125 = 48.5 \text{ cycles}$$

$$\text{AMAT} = 4 + 0.05 \times 48.5 = 6.425 \text{ cycles}$$

Global miss rates are $g_1 = m_1 = 0.05$, $g_2 = m_1 m_2 = 0.015$, $g_3 = m_1 m_2 m_3 = 0.00675$. The flat form must agree:

$$4 + 0.05(11) + 0.015(35) + 0.00675(200) = 4 + 0.55 + 0.525 + 1.35 = 6.425 \ \checkmark$$

Of the 2.425 cycles added on top of the guaranteed L1 hit time, 1.35 — well over half — comes from the $0.675\%$ of references that reach DRAM, even though that path is taken on fewer than 7 references in a thousand. The lesson is structural, not numerical: a change to $m_1$ multiplies every term below it, while a change deep in the hierarchy is scaled down by the small global rate that reaches it.

pitfalls: **Confusing local and global miss rate.** A 30–40% local L2 miss rate is routine; the corresponding global rate $g_2 = m_1 m_2$ is typically under 2%. The recursive AMAT formula takes local rates, the flat sum takes global ones — mixing them inflates or deflates the answer by an order of magnitude.

**Double-charging or dropping the hit time.** $\text{AMAT} = T_h + m T_p$ already pays $T_h$ on every access, hit or miss, because the lookup that discovers a miss is itself the hit-time cost. Writing $(1-m)T_h + m T_p$ silently drops $T_h$ from the miss path.

**Treating the miss penalty as one constant across a hierarchy.** In a multi-level cache there is no single penalty: an L1 miss costs $\text{AMAT}_2$, which depends on $m_2$, $m_3$ and DRAM latency. "The" miss penalty is only well-defined for a single-level cache.

**Assuming bigger blocks are strictly better.** They cut the compulsory miss rate as $1/B$, but at fixed capacity they leave fewer lines — hurting temporal locality — and they raise the miss penalty via a longer transfer. 64 bytes is a compromise, not a limit case.

**Reading AMAT as wall-clock time.** AMAT is an average latency; an out-of-order core overlaps independent misses with useful work and with each other. Code with high memory-level parallelism absorbs misses AMAT charges in full; a pointer-chasing loop, where each miss depends on the last, cannot. AMAT ranks designs — it does not predict runtime by itself.

**Ignoring that associativity trades hit time for miss rate, not for free.** More ways per set genuinely lowers conflict misses, but every extra comparator and replacement-state bit is paid on every access via hit time, which is why L1 stays at low associativity while L3 can afford 16-way.
applications: **The CS:APP cache lab**, assigned in CENG331: build an $(S,E,B)$ cache simulator from an address trace and report hits, misses and evictions, then reduce a matrix transpose's miss count under a fixed cache — the loop-order and blocking material applied directly to code.

**Tuned BLAS libraries** (OpenBLAS, BLIS, Intel MKL) choose GEMM tile sizes from exactly this model — one tile dimension sized to fit L1, an outer tile sized to fit L2 — turning the same $O(N^3)$ arithmetic into an order-of-magnitude speedup purely by cutting the miss rate.

**Hardware performance counters** (`perf stat -e cache-references,cache-misses,LLC-load-misses`) measure $m_1$ and $g_3$ on real runs, turning AMAT from a formula into a live diagnosis of whether a slow loop is memory-bound at all.

**Database storage engines** size units of work to the hierarchy: column-store execution processes vectors of a few thousand values so a batch stays resident in L2, and B-tree/B+-tree node sizes are chosen so one node occupies a small, cache-line-aligned number of blocks.

**Cache-line-aware kernel data structures.** Hot per-CPU structures in the Linux kernel are declared cache-line-aligned so two cores never share a 64-byte line; without it, coherence traffic from false sharing looks exactly like an inexplicably high miss rate.
exam_focus: The 2018 CENG331 final gave a direct-mapped cache with 4 sets and 2-byte blocks and asked for a filled hit/miss grid over a 5×5 char matrix summed column-wise — graders expect the block-and-set arithmetic worked by hand for each of the 25 accesses, not just the final miss count.

The last CENG331 quiz combined a cache and a TLB on one IA32 system (direct-mapped cache, 16-byte blocks, 1 KB pages, 8-entry direct-mapped TLB, one-level page table) and asked for TLB misses and L1 misses for a full N×N array traversal, then a separate miss count for a loop that alternates between two fixed elements — testing whether those two addresses collide in the same set.

The AMAT drill the slides drive home by heart: hit time 1 cycle, miss penalty 100 cycles, 97% hits gives 4 cycles and 99% hits gives 2 cycles — offered explicitly as the reason the course reports miss rate rather than hit rate.

The Core i7 numbers the slides quote (L1 4 cycles, L2 11 cycles, L3 30–40 cycles) differ slightly from CS:APP's own textbook figure for the same processor (10 and 40–75); on a METU exam, use the slide numbers and state the assumption rather than the book's.

self_check.question: A classmate says an L2 cache with a 35% miss rate must be poorly designed. What is wrong with that reasoning, and which number should they have quoted instead?
self_check.answer:
35% is very likely the **local** L2 miss rate — misses at L2 divided only by the references that reached L2, i.e., that already missed L1. L1 filters out everything with easy locality, so what arrives at L2 is the hard residue; a local rate of 25–40% is ordinary, not a design flaw.

The rate that describes the *program's* overall behavior is the **global** rate $g_2 = m_1 m_2$. With a typical $m_1 = 5\%$, $g_2 = 0.05 \times 0.35 = 1.75\%$ — fewer than two references in a hundred get past L2 at all. Judging the cache design further requires folding in the hit-time cost too: a lower local miss rate bought at the price of a much higher L2 hit time can raise AMAT even while lowering $g_2$, so neither rate alone settles the question.

self_check.question: For an array of `int` (4 bytes) with a 64-byte block, what is the predicted compulsory miss rate for a stride-1 scan, and for a scan with stride $N=20$ elements? Verify both with the code listing's model, adjusting `ELEM` and `BLOCK`.
self_check.answer:
Stride-1: predicted miss rate is $\text{sizeof(elem)}/B = 4/64 = 0.0625$, i.e., one miss every 16 elements (16 ints fit in one 64-byte block). Stride-$N$ with $N=20$: the per-step address jump is $20 \times 4 = 80$ bytes, which already exceeds the 64-byte block, so every access lands in a different block and the predicted miss rate is $1.0$.

Running the listing's `trial()` with `ELEM=4`, `BLOCK=64` and the stride built into the row/column addressing (row-major for the first case; for the second, index with a fixed stride of 20 elements instead of `N`) reproduces both numbers exactly, because the model directly implements "hit iff the current access falls in the same block as the previous one," which is precisely the $1/N \approx 0$ assumption the slides state.

self_check.question: You can spend a fixed engineering budget on exactly one of two changes to the hierarchy in the worked example: (A) lower $m_1$ from 5% to 3% at no change to $T_{h,1}$, or (B) lower $T_{\text{DRAM}}$ from 200 to 120 cycles at no change to any miss rate. Which gives the larger AMAT reduction, and why does the answer generalize?
self_check.answer:
Baseline AMAT is 6.425 cycles (from $\text{AMAT}_2=48.5$).

**(A) $m_1 = 3\%$:** $\text{AMAT}_2$ is unchanged at 48.5, so $\text{AMAT}_A = 4 + 0.03 \times 48.5 = 5.455$ cycles — a reduction of 0.97 cycles.

**(B) $T_{\text{DRAM}} = 120$:** rebuild the recursion: $\text{AMAT}_3 = 35 + 0.45 \times 120 = 89$, $\text{AMAT}_2 = 11 + 0.30 \times 89 = 37.7$, $\text{AMAT}_B = 4 + 0.05 \times 37.7 = 5.885$ cycles — a reduction of 0.54 cycles.

(A) wins, and the reason generalizes: $m_1$ sits at the top of the recursion and multiplies the *entire* $\text{AMAT}_2$ subtree below it, so a percentage-point change there is leveraged by everything the hierarchy does further down. $T_{\text{DRAM}}$ sits at the bottom and is reached on only $g_3 = m_1 m_2 m_3 \approx 0.7\%$ of references, so even a 40% cut to it barely moves AMAT. This is the same structural reason software fixes to the top-level miss rate usually beat hardware fixes to the bottom-level latency.

key_points: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty; hit time is paid on every access, penalty only on misses.
In a multi-level cache the penalty of level k is the AMAT of level k+1 — a recursion, not a constant.
Local miss rate divides by references reaching that level; global miss rate divides by all CPU references.
Core i7: L1 32 KB 8-way 4 cyc, L2 256 KB 8-way 11 cyc, L3 8 MB 16-way 30-40 cyc; B = 64 B everywhere.
Larger blocks cut compulsory misses but raise miss penalty; higher associativity cuts conflict misses but raises hit time.
Stride-1 array traversal misses at rate sizeof(elem)/B; a large stride misses at rate 1.
tagline: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, applied recursively L1→L2→L3→DRAM, so a point at the top outweighs a big latency cut at the bottom.
tldr: Cache performance reduces to one equation, $\text{AMAT} = T_h + m \cdot T_p$, applied recursively down the hierarchy: each level's miss penalty is the next level's AMAT. Because $m_1$ multiplies every term below it while deeper latencies are reached only through a shrinking global miss rate, improving the top-level miss rate usually beats improving a lower level's latency. Block size trades compulsory misses against miss penalty; associativity trades conflict misses against hit time — the Core i7's 8-way L1/L2 and 16-way L3 is that trade-off made concrete.
